overview: Bangladesh became independent in 1971 after the liberation war. Its earlier twentieth-century history includes British Bengal and the eastern wing of Pakistan. This imported record starts in 1945, before Bangladesh was a sovereign state, and projects a later outline backward. Its available polygons skip 1960 to 1994 and stop at 2020 despite an open-ended index. Those gaps do not represent independence or disappearance. Bengal, British Raj and Pakistan have separate cards.

periods.title: Before partition
periods.summary: The mapped area was still under British rule; Bangladesh was not yet a separate state.

periods.title: Eastern Pakistan
periods.summary: Partition made this region Pakistan’s eastern wing; language, representation and unequal power became major political issues.

periods.title: Independent Bangladesh
periods.summary: The liberation war established an independent republic, followed by constitutional, political and social changes.

items.text: Partition in 1947 placed the eastern and western parts of Pakistan on opposite sides of India, more than a thousand miles apart. Governmental and economic power was concentrated in the west. Being part of one country did not remove the distance or disagreements over how resources and political authority should be shared.

The language movement made everyday speech a constitutional issue. Activists demanded recognition for Bangla alongside Urdu. On 21 February 1952 police killed demonstrators in Dhaka. Their deaths became central to the movement’s memory and to a broader struggle over whose language and voice would count in public institutions.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s Awami League won the majority in Pakistan’s 1970 national election, but power was not transferred to it. A Pakistani military crackdown in March 1971 was followed by the liberation war. Bengali resistance forces and Indian troops entered Dhaka in December; Pakistan’s forces there surrendered on 16 December 1971.

The constitution took effect in December 1972, establishing parliamentary institutions. Independence did not bring stable government immediately: Mujib was killed in a 1975 military coup, and military rule followed through successive changes of leadership. A constitutional change in 1991 restored parliamentary government, with executive authority centred on the prime minister.

Article 3 of the 1972 constitution reads “প্রজাতন্ত্রের রাষ্ট্রভাষা বাংলা৷” in the official online Bangla edition. A simplified Latin reading is “prajatantrer rashtrabhasha Bangla”; the official English meaning is “The state language of the Republic is Bangla.” This is a modern digital reproduction of the constitutional text, not a photograph of its original page.

The constitution describes the national emblem using familiar plants: a water lily, ears of rice and jute leaves, together with stars. Fields and wetlands thus appear in the country’s official imagery. A symbol on a government document can also be a miniature lesson about the landscape people work in.

Jamdani weavers around Dhaka create fine cotton cloth on handlooms, inserting patterns as they weave. The designs are built into the fabric through an additional discontinuous weft, rather than printed afterward. UNESCO describes home workshops where skills pass from parents to children, supported by spinners, dyers and people who prepare the looms.

In Sylhet, Shital Pati makers split murta stems into strips and weave them into mats used for sitting, sleeping or prayer. UNESCO’s account describes both men and women preparing materials, with women particularly involved in weaving. Learning happens in families and cooperatives. Furniture can begin as a bundle of carefully prepared plant strips.

In parts of Gopalganj, Pirojpur and Barisal, farmers grow vegetables on floating beds called dhap. Layers of water hyacinth and other plant material support the beds, with bamboo helping their structure and decomposing upper layers feeding the crops. Okra, gourds, spinach and aubergines can grow above flooded ground. The vegetable patch has learned to float.

A floating garden changes with the seasons. When floodwaters recede, farmers dismantle the beds and spread the decomposed material on land for winter cultivation. The old garden becomes food for the next one. FAO’s account documents a cycle linking flood-season vegetables, compost and dry-season farming, rather than a permanent floating island.

Factory clothing became a major part of Bangladesh’s economy alongside older weaving skills. An ILO report records that ready-made garments supplied more than 80 percent of export earnings in 2013 to 2014, employing about four million people, a majority women. These are dated figures, but they show how strongly overseas wardrobes became linked to Bangladeshi workplaces.

The Rana Plaza building collapse in 2013 exposed deadly failures in workplace safety. Inspections and training followed. In a 2018 ILO account, a garment-factory manager describes changing how chemicals were stored after safety training, then helping train colleagues. Safer work involved buildings, electrical systems and everyday practices, with further improvements still needed.

Research in Dhaka and Calcutta helped establish oral rehydration therapy during the 1960s. Carefully measured fluids containing glucose and salts could help patients replace water lost through severe diarrhoea. A Dhaka study published in 1968 greatly reduced the need for intravenous fluid in its adult cholera patients. This was an international research achievement with important work in what was then East Pakistan.

BRAC began in 1972 with relief and rehabilitation in Sulla, helping communities rebuild after the war. During the 1980s its oral therapy extension programme taught women about treating diarrhoeal dehydration. Sharing medical knowledge with families was part of the achievement: a laboratory discovery had to reach the people caring for sick children.

BRAC’s education programme began in 1985 with twenty-two one-room schools. Its three-year primary course aimed to reach children who had missed school or dropped out, with particular attention to girls. A small classroom close to a community could open a route back into learning.

In 1993 Bangladeshi television introduced UNICEF’s fictional nine-year-old Meena in Count Your Chickens, a story about her wish to attend school. Her brother Raju and pet parrot Mithu joined the adventures. Children helped shape the character through extensive consultation. A cartoon girl and a bird became a way for families to discuss education and fair treatment.

A 2022 UNICEF story follows sixteen-year-old Eti in Monohorpur, Satkhira. Her family moved their toilet closer to the house and upgraded its concrete rings, slab and water seal. The 3,300-taka cost was paid in instalments. Eti felt safer using it at night: sanitation also involved privacy, location and whether someone needed to accompany her.

At a Pirojpur school described by UNICEF in 2022, girls could obtain free menstrual pads from a hygiene corner. An honesty shop also sold pads and stationery, with pupils expected to leave the correct payment themselves. These practical arrangements helped make menstruation something students could discuss and manage while attending lessons.

After the devastating 1970 cyclone, the Cyclone Preparedness Programme began in 1972 and became a joint government and Red Crescent programme in 1973. Volunteers carry official weather warnings into communities and help people evacuate, reach shelters and receive first aid. Preparing together turns a forecast into actions that neighbours can actually take.

ending.text: Bangladesh continues as an independent republic. Coups and constitutional changes concern its government, not the disappearance of its people. The imported record’s missing 1960 to 1994 polygons and last snapshot in 2020 are gaps in this map dataset, not the country’s beginning or ending.
